title: In the hand of God (Wisdom 3:1–9)
hook: the souls of the just are in the hand of God, read at many funerals

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judith told the elders they couldn't put God on a deadline, and walked out the gate. Your line was a widow saved the city. Did you say your honest sentence? Day four hundred forty.

"But the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them." If you've been to a few Catholic funerals, you may have heard that sentence read from the lectern while you stared at a coffin and tried not to cry. It's one of the most often chosen first readings at a Catholic funeral. Many people hear it only there, at the worst moment, without knowing where it comes from. It comes from one of the seven books we met this week: the Book of Wisdom.
screen: `READ FROM THE LECTERN.` → `AT THE WORST MOMENT.` → `FROM THE BOOK OF WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Wisdom speaks in the voice of King Solomon, but it was written in Greek, probably in Alexandria in Egypt, in the century or so before Christ, by a Jewish teacher using Solomon's voice, as writers of the time often did. Chapter two gives the other side first. It lets the ungodly speak, and they sound very modern. Life is short and then nothing, they say. Let's enjoy ourselves, and if a just man gets in our way and makes us feel bad, let's crush him and see if his God saves him. Then chapter three answers. The souls of the just are in the hand of God. And the Douay goes on: "In the sight of the unwise they seemed to die: and their departure was taken for misery: And their going away from us, for utter destruction: but they are in peace." Seemed. To someone looking from outside, it's the end, a loss, a ruin. But they are in peace. The writer says their hope is full of immortality. God tested them like gold in a furnace, and received them like an offering. And at their visitation, they'll shine, and run like sparks through stubble. This is one of the clearest places in the Old Testament where hope reaches past death, and you can see why the Church reaches for it at funerals, and on the feasts of martyrs. The image is the simplest one there is. A hand. Not a cloud, not a throne, not a distant place. A hand, the way you'd hold something small and precious so nothing can get at it.
screen: `WRITTEN IN GREEK, IN SOLOMON'S VOICE.` · `THE UNGODLY SPEAK FIRST.` · `THEY SEEMED TO DIE.` · `GOLD IN THE FURNACE, SPARKS IN STUBBLE.` · then, large: `BUT THEY ARE IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who has died. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind. A grandparent, a friend, a parent, a child, someone whose funeral you remember, or someone whose funeral you missed. Say their name quietly. Picture their hands, if you can remember them. Then picture those hands held in a larger hand, safe, so that nothing can touch them now. If you pray, you can pray for them; many Catholics use the old prayer that begins eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord. If you don't, just hold their name for a while. The bell holds the time.
In the hand of God. Wisdom's promise about the just who have died: they seemed to die, but they are in peace, held where no torment can touch them. Today's word.
screen: `IN THE HAND OF GOD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in the hand of god. Today, say the name of the person you remembered out loud to someone else, and tell one thing about them. Day four hundred forty.

howItsDone: Wisdom 3:1–9 is among the Old Testament readings families most often choose for a Catholic funeral, and it is also read on feasts of martyrs and on All Souls' Day.

original.note: Greek: in the hand of God, from Wisdom 3:1, a book written in Greek.

trapdoor: what you thought: a funeral reading.
what it means: an answer to people who say death is the end: the just only seemed to die; they are held in God's hand, in peace.
what a scholar hears: a Greek book from Alexandria in Solomon's voice, one of the Old Testament's clearest hopes beyond death; its phrase 'full of immortality' uses athanasia.
